params.question: According to C.E.A. Winslow's 1920 definition, what is the defining focus of public health?

answers.text: Diagnosing and treating disease in individual patients

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: This describes clinical medicine. Winslow's definition specifically emphasises prevention and organised community efforts, not individual patient care.

answers.text: Preventing disease and promoting health through organised community efforts

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Winslow defined public health as both a science and an art, centred on preventing disease, prolonging life, and promoting health through organised community action.

answers.text: Developing new drugs and surgical techniques through clinical research

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Pharmaceutical and surgical research belongs to biomedical science. Public health focuses on population-level prevention through organised community efforts.

answers.text: Providing curative care to underserved communities through mobile clinics

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: While mobile clinics serve underserved populations, curative care is a clinical function. Winslow's definition centres on prevention and health promotion at the community level.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review Winslow's definition. Public health is the science and art of preventing disease, prolonging life, and promoting health through organised community efforts — not individual clinical care.

Well done. Winslow's definition captures two essential features: public health is both a science and an art, and it works through organised community efforts — its population focus and preventive orientation set it apart from clinical medicine.

interactions.label: The Lalonde Report (1974) was a landmark shift in understanding disease causatio

params.question: The Lalonde Report (1974) was a landmark shift in understanding disease causation. Which of the following best describes what this framework identified?

answers.text: A model centred exclusively on genetic and biological causes of disease

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: This describes the older biomedical model. The Lalonde Report was significant precisely because it moved beyond this narrow biological focus to recognise multiple determinant categories.

answers.text: A classification of diseases according to the organ systems they affect

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Organ-system classification is used in clinical pathology. The Lalonde Report addressed disease causation at the population level, identifying four broad categories of health determinants.

answers.text: A framework identifying human biology, environment, lifestyle, and health-care organisation as four broad determinant categories

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. The Lalonde Report established that health is shaped by biology, environment, lifestyle, and health-care organisation — a major departure from the purely biomedical model that focused on biology alone.

answers.text: A system for ranking communicable diseases by their case-fatality rates

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The Lalonde Report did not rank diseases. It redefined how we understand what causes disease, showing that multiple determinant categories interact to produce health and illness.

overallFeedback.feedback: The Lalonde Report (Canada, 1974) identified four broad categories — human biology, environment, lifestyle, and health-care organisation — as determinants of health, replacing the older model that focused on biology alone.

Exactly right. The Lalonde Report shifted thinking from a purely biomedical model to a multifactorial one, recognising that human biology, environment, lifestyle, and health-care organisation all determine health outcomes.

params.question: In the natural history of disease, the 'iceberg phenomenon' (Gordon, 1952) refers to which concept?

answers.text: The progressive worsening of a disease from mild to severe stages over time

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: This describes disease progression within an individual. The iceberg phenomenon is about the ratio of visible (diagnosed) to invisible (sub-clinical) cases across a population.

answers.text: The geographic spread of a disease from one community to adjacent regions

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: This describes disease diffusion. The iceberg phenomenon refers to the hidden mass of sub-clinical cases that coexist with the smaller number of clinically apparent ones.

answers.text: The large proportion of sub-clinical, undiagnosed cases hidden beneath the smaller visible fraction of diagnosed cases

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Just as most of an iceberg lies below the waterline, diseases like tuberculosis, dengue, and poliomyelitis have far more sub-clinical cases than clinically diagnosed ones.

answers.text: The tendency of epidemics to appear suddenly and then subside after a peak

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: This describes the epidemic curve pattern. The iceberg phenomenon specifically addresses the proportion of disease that remains undiagnosed in the sub-clinical phase of pathogenesis.

overallFeedback.feedback: The iceberg phenomenon means that diagnosed, symptomatic cases are only the visible tip; the much larger mass of sub-clinical, undiagnosed cases lies hidden beneath — important for TB, dengue, poliomyelitis, and COVID-19.

Well done. The iceberg phenomenon highlights that in many diseases the sub-clinical, undiagnosed cases vastly outnumber those that present clinically — a critical concept for understanding disease surveillance and prevention.

interactions.label: Providing health information alone through posters and pamphlets is generally su

params.question: Providing health information alone through posters and pamphlets is generally sufficient to produce lasting behaviour change in a population.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: Information alone rarely changes behaviour. The knowledge-action gap exists because behaviour is driven by self-efficacy, social norms, perceived benefit, and access to healthier options — not just awareness. Multi-pronged approaches are needed.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct — this statement is false. The video explains that information-only campaigns consistently fall short because they do not address the deeper drivers of behaviour: self-efficacy, social norms, perceived benefit, and accessibility of healthier alternatives.

interactions.label: Which of the following is classified as a 'positive health indicator' — one that

params.question: Which of the following is classified as a 'positive health indicator' — one that measures actual well-being rather than disease or death?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The infant mortality rate is a mortality indicator. It measures premature death in the first year of life, which is the opposite of a positive health measure.
Tuberculosis prevalence is a morbidity indicator. It quantifies the burden of a specific disease in the population, not the presence of good health.
Correct. Life expectancy at birth reflects the overall health and development of a population by measuring expected years of life — it captures well-being, not disease or death.
Years lived with disability (YLD) is a disability indicator. It quantifies the non-fatal burden of disease and functional limitation — the opposite of a positive health measure.

overallFeedback.feedback: Positive health indicators measure actual good health and functional capacity — not the absence of disease. Life expectancy at birth is the classic example, reflecting overall population well-being rather than illness or death.

Exactly right. Positive health indicators like life expectancy capture functional capacity and well-being, distinguishing them from mortality, morbidity, and disability indicators that measure disease burden.
